analysis.one_liner: Taxes every stock, bond, and derivatives trade to fund public health, infrastructure, and education programs.
analysis.headline: The bill went to the House Ways and Means Committee in May 2019 and died there, with 33 cosponsors and no hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a small tax on every purchase of stocks (0.5%), bonds (0.1%), and derivatives (0.005%) traded in or by people in the United States. It exempts new stock issues and municipal bonds, and it refunds the tax to households making under $50,000 a year. The revenue, estimated by supporters in the hundreds of billions annually, would fund health care, infrastructure, clean energy, college affordability, and global health programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households, who are largely exempted through the refundable credit for anyone making under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples), and everyone who benefits from the public programs the revenue could fund: expanded Medicare and Medicaid, water and transportation infrastructure, housing assistance, clean energy, free college, and international HIV and health programs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill says a small tax on every financial trade could generate hundreds of billions of dollars annually for jobs, health care, infrastructure, and climate programs [S3].
Individuals making under $50,000 ($75,000 married) get a full credit for any tax they paid on their own trades, so the burden falls mainly on large and frequent traders [S2] [S3].
The bill's findings argue a transactions tax would curb high-frequency trading, which it says is up to 70% of the market and adds volatility without serving real liquidity needs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wall Street trading firms, banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency traders, who would pay on every transaction; some of the cost would also trickle into the returns of ordinary investors through retirement funds and brokerage accounts, though the bill argues that impact would be negligible for a typical investor. New stock offerings and tax-exempt municipal bonds are excluded, so companies raising capital and state and local borrowing are spared.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency traders

drawbacks.text: Trading firms generally pass transaction costs through to customers, so some of the tax would land in the retirement accounts and brokerage fees of ordinary savers, and some trading could move to foreign exchanges to avoid it. The bill tries to counter this by covering any purchase where a buyer or seller is a US person [S3].

High-volume traders, including market makers who buy and sell thousands of times a day, would face sharply higher costs, which could widen bid-ask spreads for all investors if those traders reduce activity [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the revenue estimates hold, the programs funded would be a large public benefit and the direct tax burden on a typical household with under $50,000 income would be zeroed out by the credit. The main cost is uncertainty about how much trading volume and investor return the tax would shave, and those costs would fall partly on retirement savers. The bill's premise rests on the idea that taxing high-frequency speculation both raises money and improves market stability; economists have long debated that second point.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Barbara Lee introduced the bill on May 22, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee, which holds jurisdiction over tax bills [S1] [S5].
Thirty-three House Democrats cosponsored it, but no further action was ever taken; the committee never scheduled it, and the full action history shows only the introduction and referral [S4] [S5].
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, without the bill reaching a vote, so it was discarded when the new Congress began [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial trading firms, banks, and hedge funds are better off: every trade they made over the two years remained untaxed, and the revenue never materialized for the public programs it would have funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trading firms, banks, and hedge funds

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Inclusive Prosperity Act and brought it to the House floor process with 19 original cosponsors.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote in the 20 months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill never reached a vote that would have shown broader support.

industries.industry: Wall Street trading firms and hedge funds
industries.note: Every stock, bond, and derivatives purchase they make would be taxed, hitting high-volume and high-frequency traders hardest. Their interest in the bill runs against the public's only in the sense that the tax would fund public programs; they have no direct gain from the bill failing, but they are the ones the tax targets.

The bill's findings explicitly target high-frequency trading, which it says makes up as much as 70% of market volume. A tax on every transaction makes their business model, which depends on enormous trade counts, dramatically more expensive.

These firms would be legally responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on trades on their facilities, adding compliance work, and reduced trading volume could cut their transaction revenue. On the other hand, the bill assigns collection duties to them rather than requiring individual small investors to file.

Fund investors' trades would be taxed, and some cost would flow into fund returns, but low-income households are refunded through the credit and the bill claims a negligible impact on the average investor. Funds themselves are not directly taxed on trades for investors beyond the transaction tax itself.

industries.industry: Municipal bond market and companies raising capital
industries.note: New securities issues and tax-exempt state and local bonds are explicitly exempted, so public-works borrowing and corporate capital raising are untouched.
